name: Chromalex
description: A broad-spectrum immunosuppressant engineered specifically for cybernetic implant tolerance, targeting the T-cell response pathways that identify synthetic materials as foreign bodies. Chromalex is the most widely prescribed drug in GLMZ — missing more than three consecutive doses can trigger acute rejection syndrome, causing the body to violently attack implanted chrome. Available in generic and premium formulations.
effects: sustained immune tolerance of cybernetic implants
reduction of chronic low-grade inflammation at implant sites
stabilization of the organic-synthetic interface membrane
side_effects: mild fatigue in first two weeks of use
liver enzyme elevation with long-term use
rebound hyperimmune response if abruptly discontinued
rare: implant micro-encapsulation if dose is inconsistent
street_price: Φ8–Φ22 per day depending on formulation
cultural_context: Chromalex or its generics are as mundane as vitamins in 2200 — anyone with chrome takes it, full stop. On the Shelf, missing doses because you can't afford them is a quiet crisis. Tier 1 clinics ration it, and Shelf residents sometimes share pills, cutting them in half and hoping it's enough. Tier 4-5 users take Chromalex Premium, a time-release sublingual formula with added anti-inflammatory compounds. The phrase 'forgot my chrome peace' is slang for being dangerously distracted or off-balance.
story_hooks: A Shelf-based fixer's chrome is beginning to reject — they have four days before their arm starts seizing. Their supplier was just killed and the nearest clinic is in Tier 2 territory with a three-day waiting list.
Someone is systematically poisoning a neighborhood's Chromalex supply with a compound that accelerates rejection rather than suppressing it — the chrome in the district is turning on its owners.
A Novafold whistleblower claims the generic formulation is intentionally less effective than clinical trials show, forcing Tier 1-2 users into more frequent purchases of the 'enhanced' version.
